thread.title: Guest Column: When politics stops seeing people as human
thread.title_full: Guest Column: When politics stops seeing people as human

author: Nicolas Hanhan, instructional technology coordinator at Arizona Western College
title: Guest Column: When politics stops seeing people as human
text:
In a school hallway, difference can become a target. A student whose body moved in ways beyond his control became an easy subject of mockery. Classmates laughed at what they did not understand. Some avoided him. Others reduced him to a nickname, stripping away individuality and dignity.
What was happening in those moments was not just bullying. It was something deeper. It was dehumanization.
Dehumanization begins when a person is no longer seen as fully human, but instead as a problem, a joke, or a label. In a classroom, it leads to exclusion and cruelty. In society, it lays the groundwork for something far more dangerous.
This pattern does not end in childhood. It evolves.
In today’s political climate, the same instinct appears in more explicit forms. A public servant with decades of military service, such as Mark Kelly, has been described in online discourse as a “traitor” or even “traitor-in-chief.”
Such language does not engage with ideas or policy differences. It reduces a person to a single, inflammatory identity. A decorated veteran and former astronaut becomes not a complex individual with a record of service, but a symbol of betrayal.
This is not simply disagreement. It is dehumanization.
Similarly, rhetoric used by President Donald Trump has at times framed opponents as “enemies,” while entire nations, including Iran, are described in broad and absolute terms. These are not neutral descriptions. They are labels that compress millions of individuals into a single threatening image.
When language shifts from disagreement to condemnation of identity, the consequences are predictable. People stop listening. They begin categorizing.
This pattern is not limited to one country or one political ideology. Across regions and conflicts, similar language emerges. In parts of the Middle East, groups such as Hezbollah have labeled opponents as “traitors” or collaborators, turning disagreement into moral betrayal. In such frameworks, those who are not aligned are not simply wrong. They are disloyal, dangerous, or deserving of punishment.
The language changes. The pattern does not.
History shows that this pattern is neither new nor harmless. In many of the darkest chapters of the modern world, dehumanizing language came first. Before policies were enacted or violence carried out, groups were described as dangerous, inferior, or disloyal.
What begins as words rarely ends there.
The distance between a schoolyard insult and a political statement may seem vast, but the underlying mechanism is the same. Both rely on turning difference into deficiency and identity into stigma.
Yet the same process can be interrupted.
Recognizing humanity in others requires intention. It requires resisting the urge to label, dismiss, or reduce. It requires choosing understanding over assumption, even when difference feels unfamiliar.
Within the Orthodox Christian tradition, the human person is not defined by politics, nationality, or ideology, but by bearing the image of God. To reduce another person to a label is to ignore that image.
In a widely shared message, an Orthodox priest offered a challenge that cuts across political lines:
“If you’re a Republican that hates Democrats, you need to learn to love Democrats. If you’re a Democrat who hates Republicans, you need to learn to love Republicans.”
The message is simple, but difficult.
It is not a call to agreement. It is a call to recognition. Even in deep disagreement, the other person does not cease to be human.
A society that normalizes dehumanizing language, whether in casual conversation or political discourse, risks normalizing the harm that follows. Words do not exist in isolation. They prepare the ground for action.
The responsibility, then, is shared.
To speak differently. To see differently. To refuse the reduction of any person to less than human.
Because dehumanization does not begin with actions. It begins with words.
